exam_guide_revision: Reviewed anti-boring v4, 2026-09-26. Full learning and question editorial audit completed; weak/generic prompts and distractors were rewritten while preserving compatibility.

learning_design.unlock_rule: All learning reveals are required. Each node moves quickly through a concrete problem, the obvious failure/waste, the maintained state or invariant that fixes it, the pattern name, a different real-world transfer, and one quick check.
learning_design.mastery_note: The goal is not to enjoy studying algorithms. The goal is to recognize the structure fast enough that an unfamiliar problem starts to look like a problem you have already solved.

authoring_notes: Anti-boring rule set: no optional reveals; no definition-first nodes; no university-course voice; no fake corporate narrative; start with code/data/workload; expose the waste or bug; name the useful state; then name the pattern; finish with transfer.

modules.title: Do not destroy useful sequence information

nodes.title: Before you sort or use a set, ask what the sequence itself is telling you

reveal.text: A log function must return the FIRST failed request index and duplicates are meaningful. You are learning to recognize when order, position, adjacency, or multiplicity are part of the answer.

reveal.text: Converting the log to a set keeps unique values but destroys first position, duplicates, and adjacency.

spans.text: the transformation throws away sequence information the output needs

reveal.text: Name the required sequence semantics first. If you need first/index/contiguous/original order, preserve positions while you optimize.

spans.text: the positional information the contract still requires

reveal.text: Sequence-semantics check. Trigger: the prompt contains first, last, index, contiguous, adjacent, original order, or duplicate count

reveal.text: A longest contiguous burst and a first duplicate index are different problems, but both fail if you turn the sequence into an unordered set.

spans.text: position-sensitive outputs require position-preserving state

reveal.text: Can a plain set answer 'where did X first occur'? Answer: No — membership survives, first position does not.

nodes.title: If the next item only needs one fact from the past, carry that one fact

annotations.explanation: The rule compares adjacent timestamps, not arbitrary history.

annotations.title: Scan order gives the earliest violation

reveal.text: Ask what the next element needs from the processed prefix. Sometimes it is just previous value, best-so-far, running min/max, or one index.

reveal.text: One-pass running state. Trigger: each new element can be evaluated using a bounded summary of what came before

nodes.title: Normalization is a business rule, not a cleanup reflex

reveal.text: Feature tags are explicitly case-insensitive and surrounding whitespace does not matter. You are learning to build canonical hash keys only when multiple input forms are defined as the same identity.

spans.text: Feature tags are explicitly case-insensitive and surrounding whitespace does not matter.
You are learning to build canonical hash keys only when multiple input forms are defined as the same identity

reveal.text: Lowercasing every identifier 'for convenience' can silently merge identities when the real contract is case-sensitive.

spans.text: normalization can corrupt identity semantics

reveal.text: Encode only the equivalence the contract grants. For these tags, `tag.strip().lower()` is valid; for case-sensitive usernames it is not.

spans.text: a canonical key that preserves exactly the intended equivalence relation

reveal.text: Intentional canonicalization. Trigger: the problem explicitly defines multiple spellings/representations as equivalent

spans.text: Intentional canonicalization
the problem explicitly defines multiple spellings/representations as equivalent

reveal.text: URLs, file paths, tags, and IDs may each have different normalization rules. The algorithmic move is the same; the equivalence rule is domain-specific.

spans.text: canonicalization must match the declared identity semantics

reveal.text: If `Alice` and `alice` are distinct usernames, should you lowercase before hashing? Answer: No — that would merge two valid identities.

spans.text: No — that would merge two valid identities.

annotations.explanation: The set answers whether the key appeared in earlier positions.

annotations.title: Check before adding
annotations.explanation: Otherwise the current item would match itself.

reveal.text: Make the set mean exactly one thing: keys from the processed history. Membership becomes expected O(1) instead of rescanning that history.

reveal.text: Idempotency keys, duplicate filenames, repeated user IDs, and graph visited-state all share the same membership skeleton.

annotations.title: Solve the equation for the missing partner
annotations.explanation: For current x, every other value except target-x is irrelevant.

annotations.title: Store what the output needs
annotations.explanation: The result needs indices, so the map stores an index.

modules.title: Reuse cumulative work instead of re-adding ranges

nodes.title: Stop re-adding the same range: store cumulative totals at boundaries

reveal.text: A dashboard loads 365 daily request counts once, then answers thousands of range-total queries. You are learning to precompute prefix boundary totals so repeated immutable range aggregation becomes O(1).

annotations.title: n values create n+1 boundaries
annotations.explanation: Boundary 0 is before the first value.

annotations.title: Reuse previous work
annotations.explanation: Each cumulative total extends the previous one instead of re-summing from zero.

reveal.text: Define `prefix[i]` as the sum of values before index i. Build once; reuse for every query.

spans.text: cumulative state at each sequence boundary

reveal.text: Prefix sum / prefix state. Trigger: many queries repeatedly aggregate overlapping portions of mostly static data

reveal.text: Daily request totals, byte deltas, revenue, counts, and any additive metric share the same cumulative-boundary skeleton.

nodes.title: Range sum is subtraction, not another loop

reveal.text: For `[4,7,2,5]`, the dashboard asks for the half-open range `[1,3)`. You are learning to use a consistent boundary convention to turn a range query into two prefix lookups.

spans.text: For `[4,7,2,5]`, the dashboard asks for the half-open range `[1,3)`.

reveal.text: Re-summing `7+2` works for one query but repeats work across thousands of overlapping ranges.

spans.text: each query performs aggregation that was already encoded in cumulative state

reveal.text: With `prefix[i] = sum(values[0:i])`, the answer is `prefix[r] - prefix[l]`. For this range: 13 - 4 = 9.

spans.text: left and right cumulative boundaries

reveal.text: Prefix difference. Trigger: you need aggregate state for a half-open interval of static data
